notes: darwin-origin/ch11-12: Hawks looking out for tired birds; hawks on the English coast destroying carrier-pigeons; hawks disgorging pellets.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Darwin's 'fishing-eagles' at the Zoological Gardens could be sea-eagles (Haliaeetus, Accipitridae) or the osprey (Pandion, Pandionidae); resolved to the order containing both. 'different birds of prey' also includes owls, which have their own record.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: Generic 'fish'/'fishes' (incl. fish with swimbladders and electric fishes); Darwin's electric fishes also include Torpedo (Chondrichthyes). GBIF match API returned HIGHERRANK; class Actinopterygii key 204 verified at /v1/species/204. NCBI ranks it as superclass.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Darwin's 'fish' (marine faunas of Panama, fresh-water fish of distant continents, fish eating seeds) is the paraphyletic vernacular group; resolved to Actinopterygii, the class containing essentially all the freshwater and shore fishes he discusses. Sharks and rays are excluded by this resolution. species/match returned only Animalia (HIGHERRANK); key 204 taken from Wikidata P846 and verified accepted at https://api.gbif.org/v1/species/204. Current backbone does not place fish species under this class, so its occurrence count is 0.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: 'fish' is not a taxon; Thompson's examples (length–weight growth, Froude's law of swimming) are generic bony fishes, so the mention is resolved to Actinopterygii. GBIF species/match returns NONE for this name; key 204 is the accepted CLASS record in the backbone (confirmed via /species/204) but current occurrences are indexed under the fish orders directly, so occurrence/count?taxonKey=204 returns 0 and no GBIF occurrence dataset is recorded. NCBI ranks Actinopterygii as a superclass.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF match API returned HIGHERRANK (Animalia); the accepted genus Amblyopsis DeKay, 1842 (key 2401736) was taken from the alternatives and verified at /v1/species/2401736.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'Batrachians' (19th-century term for amphibians).
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Bory St. Vincent's Batrachians (frogs, toads, newts) absent from oceanic islands.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: The Aylesbury duck is a domestic breed of the mallard.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Darwin's aquarium experiment used a (domestic) duck's feet; the pond duck he observed with duck-weed on its back is also most plausibly the mallard. If a broader reading is wanted use Anatidae.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Domestic duck and wild-duck both map to the mallard. Darwin's wing/leg bone-weight comparison is claim darwin1859-ch01-04.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'a fresh-water shell like a limpet' adhering to a Dyticus.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Common and Toulouse ('Thoulouse') geese map to the domestic goose, derived from the greylag.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Frogs introduced into Madeira, the Azores and Mauritius; a frog reported on the mountains of New Zealand.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Thompson's 'honey-comb' and 'the flower for the bee' are resolved to the honey-bee genus Apis rather than to a species; the hive-bee he discusses later in the book is Apis mellifera. WoRMS AphiaID is a non-marine record (marine_only=false).
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'the bee', 'queen-bee', 'drones'.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: 'the swift' with a quoted flight speed of 20–50 ft/s; for a British author this is the common swift.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'eye of an eagle'.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Vernacular 'eagle' resolved to the genus Aquila (true eagles).
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Mentioned only indirectly through the 'spider’s web'.

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Blackwall's 'large garden-spider' in Britain is Araneus (Epeira) diadematus.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Herons devouring fish and carrying seeds; Audubon's heron with Nelumbium seeds in its stomach.

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Koltzoff's crayfish sperm material was European Astacus; vernacular 'Crayfish' resolved to family Astacidae (GBIF has no infraorder Astacidea usage).

darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'birds' of Madeira and of the Brazilian caves.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Generic references to birds and to 'the flying bird' in the flight-scaling argument.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Generic 'bird' resolved to class Aves.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'Balanidae or sessile cirripedes', 'rock barnacles'.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'camel' resolved to the genus.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Bats on almost every oceanic island; endemic bats of New Zealand, Norfolk Island, Fiji, Bonin, Carolines, Marianas, Mauritius; two North American species visiting Bermuda; Tomes on wide-ranging species.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: PBDB taxa/single?name=Chiton returns the class Polyplacophora (txn:8023), not the genus, so pbdb_taxon_no is left null.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: Darwin's own subfamily (Darwin, 1854). WoRMS AphiaID 106076 lists it as 'unaccepted' with valid name Chthamalidae (AphiaID 106059); GBIF backbone matches it only fuzzily to Chthamalidae (key 5104), so gbif_usage_key is left null. Not in NCBI, ITIS or PBDB.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Bosquet's Cretaceous (Chalk of Belgium) specimen is the point of Darwin's example.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'cirripedes', 'pedunculated cirripedes', 'hermaphrodite cirripedes'. GBIF backbone has no Cirripedia node (match API returned HIGHERRANK Animalia); NCBI ranks it as subclass.

darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Lubbock's Coccus (scale insects, Hemiptera: Coccidae). GBIF species/match returns no match for 'Coccus' because of homonyms; the genus usage 2049629 (Coccus Linnaeus, 1758, Coccidae) was looked up by key and verified. Lubbock's 1859 paper concerned Coccus hesperidum (GBIF 5712981, NCBI 538890).
darwin-origin/ch05-06: The ground woodpecker of the La Plata plains Darwin observed on the Beagle voyage.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Wollaston's Madeiran beetles and generic 'beetles'.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'coleopterous insects of Madeira'.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Shrivelled wings under soldered elytra of insular beetles; distribution of beetles compared with butterflies.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: 'Coleopterous insects of two districts' used in Darwin's large-genera tabulation.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: All domestic breeds (tumbler, carrier, fantail, pouter, barb) are C. livia.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: All of Darwin's domestic breeds (fantail, pouter, carrier, tumbler) are C. livia; the 'rock-pigeon' is the wild form. Wikidata Q42326 is the species item (P225 Columba livia).
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Seeds from the crop of a pigeon floated 30 days on salt water; carrier-pigeons killed by hawks on the English coast. Both domestic C. livia.

darwin-origin/intro-ch02: All domestic pigeon breeds (carrier, tumbler, runt, barb, pouter, turbit, Jacobin, trumpeter, laugher, fantail) and the dovecot-pigeon map to Columba livia. 'C. intermedia of Strickland' is the subspecies Columba livia intermedia (GBIF 5231827, Wikidata Q27609044).
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Stock dove, named by Darwin as a possible alternative ancestor of the domestic pigeon.

darwin-origin/intro-ch02: The 'great pigeon family' / Columbidæ, including the 'two or three other species of rock-pigeons'. WoRMS AphiaID 196065 is claimed on Wikidata but the WoRMS REST lookup returned an empty body, so it is left null.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Water-beetle that flew on board the Beagle 45 miles from land.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'quail' in a British context.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'the millions of quails which annually cross the Mediterranean'.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Conklin's dwarf and giant Crepidula and the American slipper-limpet 'now much at home on our own oyster-beds' is C. fornicata, but the text names only the genus. GBIF species/match needs kingdom=Animalia to disambiguate from a Protozoa homonym. NCBI Datasets lists no genome assembly for taxid 52628 at retrieval time.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: Falconer's 'existing crocodile' from the Siwalik (sub-Himalayan) deposits, usually identified with Crocodylus palustris or Gavialis; resolved to the order. The current GBIF backbone ranks Crocodylia as a class (key 11493978).

darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF backbone has no Crustacea node (match API returned a doubtful homonymous genus, not recorded). NCBI Taxonomy merged Crustacea (taxid 6657) into Pancrustacea (197562), which also contains Hexapoda, so ncbi_taxid is null.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: GBIF backbone has no Crustacea node (only a doubtful genus-rank homonym). NCBI esearch for 'Crustacea' resolves to Pancrustacea (taxid 197562), which NCBI lists Crustacea under; recorded with that caveat.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Dana's closely allied crustaceans of the Mediterranean and Japan; New Zealand crustacea resembling Great Britain's. GBIF backbone has no Crustacea taxon (Malacostraca, Branchiopoda etc. sit directly under Arthropoda); the match API returned the homonymous bee genus Crustacea (Apidae, key 10996236), rejected. NCBI Taxonomy merged Crustacea (taxid 6657) into the clade Pancrustacea (197562), which also contains Hexapoda, so no equivalent NCBI node exists.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: NCBI esearch for 'Cuvierina[Scientific Name]' returns taxid 2952970 (genus, gastropods); the taxid 356472 listed on Wikidata returns an empty record.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'Galeopithecus' (a synonym of Cynocephalus/Galeopterus).

names_as_written: extinct and gigantic birds of New Zealand

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Extinct New Zealand ratites. The GBIF backbone has no order Dinornithiformes (species/match returns NONE) but does have the family Dinornithidae (key 3242170, 13 descendants), which is used for the GBIF occurrence-count dataset below. ITIS has no record.

The GBIF backbone has no Dinosauria node (species/match returns NONE) and ITIS does not list it. NCBI taxid 436486 is a clade without a Linnaean rank.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Delisle's 'minute fly', the dancing flies under the ceiling and 'gnats' are all resolved to Diptera; 'gnats' could be narrowed to Nematocera/Culicidae but Thompson's usage is loose. GBIF species/match needs kingdom=Animalia to disambiguate from a plant homonym.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: English racehorses do not owe their superiority to descent from a single pair.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: All horse breeds (cart, dray, race, Arab) map to the domestic horse.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: Generic references to insects, cave-insects, neuter insects, luminous insects and British insects.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: Monotypic (Lepidosiren paradoxa); resolved to the genus as written.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'our hares and rabbits' (British); hares = Lepus (L. europaeus, L. timidus).

darwin-origin/ch09-10: GBIF has several Lingula homonyms; 2252392 (Bruguière, 1791, Brachiopoda: Lingulidae) is the brachiopod. Palaeozoic 'Lingula' records are now mostly placed in other lingulid genera.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Linnaeus's stag-beetle is Lucanus cervus; resolved to the family since Thompson gives no species.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF backbone has no subfamily rank.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Extinct litoptern named by Owen from Beagle material.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Covers 'mammals', 'mammiferous remains', 'tertiary mammals', 'fossil mammals', 'eocene Mammals'.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Absence of terrestrial mammals from oceanic islands; depth of sea and mammalian affinity; frozen mammals of Siberia.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Owen's 'large mammal' passage and the mouse-to-elephant nerve-cell series.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: Darwin's 'Mastodon' (Cuvier, 1817) is a junior synonym of Mammut Blumenbach, 1799. The La Plata 'Mastodon' is now Notiomastodon platensis (Gomphotheriidae) and Falconer's Siwalik 'mastodons' are gomphotheres/stegodonts, so the genus Mammut is the nomenclatural, not the modern systematic, resolution of the name.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: GBIF backbone has only a doubtful family-rank 'Marsupialia' (9712517), not used. NCBI esearch for 'Marsupialia' resolves to Metatheria (taxid 9263), under which NCBI lists the name; recorded with that caveat.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Carboniferous 'giant dragon-flies' (Meganeura and allies) are the extinct order Meganisoptera, not true Odonata. NCBI Taxonomy has no entry (extinct, no sequence data). GBIF also has the genus Meganeura Brongniart, 1885 (key 4682601).
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Extinct giant ground sloth.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Hard seeds pass uninjured through the digestive organs of a turkey.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: The British cockchafer is Melolontha melolontha; resolved to the genus since Thompson gives no species. ITIS has no record for the genus.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Three closely allied species of mocking-thrush each confined to its own Galapagos island.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Chatham Island = San Cristóbal; its endemic mockingbird is Mimus melanotis.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Charles Island = Floreana; its mockingbird is Mimus trifasciatus (now extirpated from Floreana itself, surviving on Champion and Gardner islets).
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'shells' (living and fossil) and 'Mollusca' are resolved to the phylum.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'Molluscs', 'molluscan genus', 'genera of molluscs'.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Darwin's generic 'shells' of marine faunas, arctic shells, and 'sea-shells' of Madeira; resolved to phylum Mollusca.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: 'Dwarfed condition of shells in the brackish waters of the Baltic' – resolved only to the phylum Mollusca.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'The mouse', 'mice'; species not specified. GBIF match API returned HIGHERRANK; the accepted genus Mus Linnaeus, 1758 (key 9800657) was verified at /v1/species/9800657. NCBI taxid 10088 is the genus (862507 is the subgenus).

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: 'the mouse' in the walking and ganglion-cell comparisons (Hardesty's figure) is taken as the house mouse. GBIF key 7429082 is the accepted species record; Wikidata's P846 value 2438780 is a GBIF synonym ('Mus musculus sp. domesticus') that redirects to 7429082.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'polecats'. GBIF match API returned HIGHERRANK; accepted genus Mustela Linnaeus, 1758 (key 2433922) verified at /v1/species/2433922.

darwin-origin/intro-ch02: GBIF treats Mustela furo Linnaeus, 1758 (usageKey 5816581) as a synonym of the accepted subspecies Mustela putorius furo (5218913); the accepted usage is recorded. Wikidata item Q178973 (ferret) carries P225 'Mustela furo'. Trait databases list only the species Mustela putorius.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Extinct ground sloth; Mylodon darwinii was named from Beagle material.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Rodent of the American type in South American waters.

names_as_written: New Zealand possesses two bats found nowhere else in the world
notes: darwin-origin/ch11-12: Darwin does not name the two New Zealand bats; the two extant endemic species are Mystacina tuberculata and Chalinolobus tuberculatus. Inferred identity.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Darwin's 'Nautilus' among 'the most ancient Silurian animals' is the broad 19th-century usage (nautiloids); resolved to the living genus as written.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Written in lower case as a vernacular; resolved to the genus Nautilus Linnaeus, 1758.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'Mustela vison'; GBIF accepted name may still be Neovison vison. GBIF backbone's accepted name is Mustela vison Schreber, 1777 (key 5218823; Neovison vison key 2433652 is a synonym); NCBI (452646) and Wikidata use Neogale vison.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: The Mammoth Cave 'cave-rat' with large eyes studied by Silliman is the Allegheny woodrat (Neotoma magister); genus used.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Guinea-fowl.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'larva of the dragon-fly'.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Musk-rat absent from South America.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin wrote 'Onites apelles' (Kirby's spelling); the species epithet is not matched in the GBIF backbone so the genus Onitis Fabricius, 1798 is used.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Campanularia integra MacGillivray, 1842 is a synonym of Orthopyxis integra (GBIF synonym key 5711670 -> accepted 5186073; WoRMS 152102 -> valid 117393).
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'our hares and rabbits' (British).
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Mentioned only as the host of 'a pathogenic micrococcus of the rabbit, M. progrediens'.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Indirect mention ('our own oyster-beds', i.e. British Ostrea edulis beds); resolved to the family.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Host of Spirochaeta balbiani; vernacular 'oysters' resolved to family Ostreidae.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'sheep' (domestic breeds).
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: All sheep breeds (ancon, merino, Leicester, Yorkshire) map to the domestic sheep.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'if we compare the distribution of butterflies and beetles'. species/match does not search superfamilies; key 1875 taken from Wikidata P846 and verified accepted at https://api.gbif.org/v1/species/1875.

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Ascaris megalocephala Cloquet, 1824 is the classical cytological name for the horse ascarid, now Parascaris equorum (Goeze, 1782); some cytogenetic material is now assigned to P. univalens. Resolved to P. equorum.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Thompson writes only 'the sparrow'; for a British author this is the house sparrow. If a genus-level reading is preferred, GBIF genus Passer is key 2492321 (not verified here). Thompson's ostrich:sparrow linear ratio of 25:1 is the worked example of claim thompson1917-ch02-06.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Peacock; Darwin gives no species, Pavo cristatus is the peafowl kept in Britain. No RefSeq assembly; GenBank chromosome-level assembly recorded.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'Puffinuria berardi' = Pelecanoides urinatrix berard(i) / P. magellani; genus used.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Dead fish stuffed with seeds given to pelicans at the Zoological Gardens.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'partridge' in a British context.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Twenty-two grains of earth from the foot of a partridge (England). The grey partridge is the only native British partridge; the introduced red-legged partridge (Alectoris rufa) cannot be excluded.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'seal'; Darwin does not distinguish eared from true seals.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'scaly ant-eaters' under 'Edentata'. GBIF match restricted to Animalia (Pholidota is also an orchid genus).
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Vernacular 'woodpecker' resolved to the family Picidae; Darwin names no species.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'green woodpeckers'.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'Saurophagus sulphuratus'.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'ourang-outang'.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's monotypic genus (Proteolepas bivincta Darwin, 1854); later regarded as a parasitic isopod larva rather than a cirripede. GBIF key 2203053 (Proteolepas Darwin, 1854) has status DOUBTFUL and is placed in Isopoda: Crinoniscidae, consistent with the reinterpretation of Darwin's specimen as an isopod. Not in NCBI Taxonomy.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF match restricted to kingdom Animalia to avoid the bacterial genus Proteus.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF backbone has no tribe rank.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Resolved only to Wikidata and the Paleobiology Database: the GBIF backbone has no Pterosauria node (species/match returns NONE) and NCBI Taxonomy has no entry for this extinct order. 'Pterodactyles' in 1917 usage covers all pterosaurs.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: Gnathodon Gray, 1831 is the preoccupied older name for the brackish-water bivalve genus now called Rangia (G. cuneatus = Rangia cuneata); Darwin cites the distribution of fossil Gnathodon in the United States. Check WoRMS synonymy before merging.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: Rein-deer. No RefSeq reference assembly; a GenBank chromosome-level assembly of the Svalbard subspecies is recorded.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Vernacular 'frog' (sperm path in the frog's egg, Roux's Rana material; Trypanosoma rotatorium host) resolved to family Ranidae.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'The rat' transported by man; species not specified.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: Includes 'flying reptiles' (pterosaurs). GBIF key 358 is a pro-parte synonym (backbone splits Reptilia into Crocodylia, Squamata, Testudines etc.); NCBI Taxonomy has no Reptilia node (paraphyletic), so ncbi_taxid is null.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: The current GBIF backbone marks Reptilia (358) as a pro-parte synonym (its contents are split among Crocodylia, Squamata, Testudines, etc.); NCBI Taxonomy has no Reptilia node.

darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'in the Galapagos Islands reptiles ... take the place of mammals'. GBIF backbone treats Reptilia (key 358) as a pro parte synonym split across the classes Squamata (11592253), Testudines and Crocodylia (11493978); no single accepted key. NCBI Taxonomy has no Reptilia node (Sauropsida 8457 includes birds).
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Genus with one species near the Straits of Magellan and another on the plains of La Plata.

names_as_written: another species of the same genus
notes: darwin-origin/ch11-12: The rhea of the plains of La Plata.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: The rhea of the plains near the Straits of Magellan (Darwin's rhea, Rhea pennata; formerly Pterocnemia pennata).
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Order shared by agouti, bizcacha, hares and rabbits (as Darwin then classified lagomorphs), coypu and capybara.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Example of organs built from very few cells (eutely).
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'Ruminants'. Not in the GBIF backbone; ITIS search returned no record.

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: 'Epidermal cells of the salamander' refers to the classical Flemming material (Salamandra maculosa = S. salamandra); resolved to genus Salamandra rather than species because Thompson gives no species.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'frogs, toads, newts'; newts are Salamandridae (Pleurodelinae).
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: 'Newt' (spermatozoa of the newt or salamander) has no genus-level resolution in the text; resolved to family Salamandridae.
thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Thompson's 'trout' (Ransom's waves; Prenant/Bouin blastomere figure) is the European brown trout, Salmo trutta; GBIF backbone does not return a class for this species.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'dung-feeding beetles' (Kirby's observation) resolved to the true dung beetle subfamily. GBIF backbone has no subfamily rank for Scarabaeinae (match API fuzzy-matched the family Scarabaeidae, key 5840, which is not recorded).

names_as_written: Ateuchus or sacred beetle of the Egyptians
notes: darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'Ateuchus or sacred beetle of the Egyptians'; Ateuchus Weber in the 19th-century sense is Scarabaeus.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'coral-producing oceans' and atolls: reef-building corals, resolved to order Scleractinia.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF key 11205692 is a backbone placeholder ranked FAMILY with no descendants; occurrence counts by this key are not meaningful. NCBI ranks Serpentes as infraorder.

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Caution on the GBIF key: the backbone has no suborder rank, and record 11205692 'Serpentes' is a stub ranked FAMILY with 0 descendants and only ~5,500 occurrences attached; most snake occurrences sit under the individual families. NCBI ranks Serpentes as an infraorder, ITIS as a suborder.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'Sessile cirripedes' = acorn barnacles. Resolved to the order Sessilia (Lamarck, 1818); WoRMS marks the order's status 'uncertain' (modern WoRMS classification uses Balanomorpha). NCBI has no Sessilia node (it uses Sessilia-free ranks under Thoracicalcarea).
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'monkey'. GBIF backbone has no infraorder rank.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'monkey' (Cuvier's claim that none occurred in the Tertiary) resolved to the simians, Simiiformes. Not in the GBIF backbone. PBDB txn:95857 is a subjective synonym of Anthropoidea (txn:40840).

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: GBIF species/match needs kingdom=Animalia to disambiguate from a Chromista homonym. ITIS 152732 is the valid order record (152733 is an invalid duplicate). Central to claim thompson1917-ch02-09 (equal absolute jump height).

thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: 'saurians' = lizards (Lacertilia), which is paraphyletic and absent from GBIF and NCBI, so resolved to Squamata. GBIF now ranks Squamata as a CLASS (key 11592253, 11.9 M occurrences); the older ORDER record 715 cited by Wikidata is still 'accepted' but carries 0 occurrences.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'Some hawks and owls bolt their prey whole'.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: The African ostrich contrasted with the American rhea.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: In 1917 the ostrich was a single species; the Somali ostrich (S. molybdophanes) was split later, so Struthio camelus sensu lato is intended.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'pig' resolved to the genus.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: 'Pigs' mapped to Sus scrofa (species); the domestic form is Sus scrofa domesticus (GBIF 9104700, NCBI 9825, Wikidata Q787).

darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin's 'logger-headed duck of South America' and 'Micropterus of Eyton'; Micropterus Eyton, 1838 is a junior homonym replaced by Tachyeres Owen, 1875. Species not determinable from the text (T. brachypterus or T. pteneres).
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'tapir' resolved to the genus. ITIS has two Tapirus records; 926066 (Brisson, 1762) is the valid one, 624930 (Brünnich, 1771) is marked invalid.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'teleostean fishes'. Not in the GBIF backbone (which has no node between Actinopterygii and orders).

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: GBIF backbone usage 793 (Testudines as ORDER under Reptilia) is flagged deleted and returns 0 occurrences; the live /species/match returns 11418114 (Testudines ranked CLASS directly under Chordata), which is used here. Rank 'order' and lineage follow Wikidata/ITIS/WoRMS.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Plateau's slow tortoise; resolved to the land-tortoise family.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Extinct notoungulate named by Owen from Darwin's Beagle material.

darwin-origin/ch09-10: The bivalve Trigonia Bruguière, 1789 (GBIF 3247984; Wikidata Q38335712), not the plant or fungus homonyms. Darwin's surviving Australian species is now placed in Neotrigonia. NCBI taxid 82140 is the bivalve genus.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Extinct; not in NCBI Taxonomy (no molecular data). ITIS search returned no record. WoRMS not queried for a wholly extinct class.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: Alpine humming-birds of South America, of strictly American forms.
thompson-growth-form/ch01-02: Example of 'stationary flight' in very small birds.

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: Paraphyletic grade; GBIF backbone still carries it as an accepted class (341). WoRMS AphiaID 794 is 'unaccepted' with no valid replacement. NCBI has no Turbellaria node (the Wikidata-listed taxid 166384 returns an empty record), so ncbi_taxid is null.
darwin-origin/ch05-06: Darwin placed the dipper in the thrush family.
darwin-origin/intro-ch02: 'Plantigrades or bear family' – resolved to Ursidae.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'anteater' resolved to the suborder Vermilingua. Not in the GBIF backbone.

darwin-origin/ch05-06: GBIF backbone has no subphylum rank. NCBI taxid 7742 (clade Vertebrata); the automatic Wikidata hit Q3556237 is the red-alga genus Vertebrata and was rejected in favour of Q25241.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: Not in the GBIF backbone. Wikidata Q25241 is the subphylum (Q3556237 is a red-alga genus homonym); WoRMS 146419 likewise is the subphylum.

thompson-growth-form/ch04-05: GBIF backbone has no Vertebrata usage (name match falls back to Animalia; the only GBIF 'Vertebrata' is a red-alga genus), so gbif_usage_key is null. NCBI 7742 (clade), WoRMS 146419 (subphylum).
darwin-origin/ch05-06: 'the wasp'.

darwin-origin/intro-ch02: 'The many foxes inhabiting different quarters of the world' resolved to the genus Vulpes; some foxes (e.g. Urocyon, Lycalopex) fall outside Vulpes, so the family Canidae is the safe upper bound.
darwin-origin/ch11-12: 'icebergs ... may have formerly transported foxes, as so frequently now happens in the arctic regions': the fox carried on arctic ice is the Arctic fox. Inferred identity.
darwin-origin/ch09-10: 'Edentata' (obsolete order) resolved to Xenarthra. GBIF backbone lists Xenarthra (10998477) as a synonym at order rank.
